headings.title: Introduction to Diarrhoea and Pharmacological Management
headings.content: Diarrhoea is characterized by an increase in the frequency, fluidity, or volume of bowel movements, representing a major public health concern globally and particularly in developing regions like Nigeria. Acute diarrhoea typically lasts less than two weeks and is usually infectious in origin, whereas chronic diarrhoea persists for four weeks or longer and often stems from non-infectious causes such as inflammatory bowel disease, malabsorption syndromes, or endocrine disorders. The primary pathophysiological mechanisms driving diarrhoea include osmotic forces drawing water into the lumen, secretory processes actively pumping electrolytes and water out, exudation of mucus and blood due to mucosal inflammation, and derangements in intestinal motility that decrease contact time for absorption. Pharmacological management aims not merely to suppress symptoms, but to restore normal fluid and electrolyte balance, prevent severe dehydration, shorten the duration of illness, and eliminate underlying pathogens when applicable. Nursing students must understand that indiscriminate use of anti-diarrhoeal drugs in infectious cases, particularly when invasive bacterial pathogens are present, can trap toxins within the gut and worsen the clinical outcome. Therefore, a comprehensive assessment distinguishing between secretory, osmotic, and inflammatory etiologies is essential before initiating any pharmacological therapy. Supportive care, fluid resuscitation, and targeted drug selection remain the cornerstones of safe and effective management in clinical practice.

headings.title: Classification of Anti-Diarrhoeal Agents
headings.content: Anti-diarrhoeal agents are broadly classified based on their primary pharmacological mechanisms of action into motility inhibitors, absorbents and adsorbents, antisecretory agents, and antimicrobials. Motility inhibitors, such as loperamide and diphenoxylate, act on the smooth muscle of the intestinal tract to slow peristalsis, thereby increasing the time available for fluid absorption. Absorbents and adsorbents, including kaolin-pectin and attapulgite, function by binding toxins, microorganisms, and excess fluid to the mucosal surface of the bowel, though their overall efficacy in severe clinical cases is often limited. Antisecretory agents, such as racecadotril, reduce the hypersecretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen without altering intestinal motility. Additionally, antimicrobial agents are utilized when a specific bacterial, viral, or protozoal pathogen is identified as the underlying cause of the diarrhoeal illness. Understanding these distinct classes allows nurses and other healthcare professionals in Nigeria to anticipate medical orders, administer medications safely, and monitor patients for therapeutic effectiveness as well as potential adverse drug reactions. Each class carries distinct indications and contraindications, making tailored pharmacological selection vital for optimal patient recovery.

headings.title: Motility Inhibitors: Mechanism and Clinical Use
headings.content: Motility inhibitors are powerful medications designed to reduce the propulsive movements of the gastrointestinal tract, effectively decreasing stool frequency and urgency. The most commonly used agent in this category is loperamide, an opioid derivative that acts on the mu-opioid receptors in the intestinal circular and longitudinal muscles without producing significant central nervous system effects at standard therapeutic doses. By inhibiting peristalsis, loperamide increases the contact time between intestinal contents and the mucosal surface, promoting greater water and electrolyte absorption. Diphenoxylate, another motility inhibitor, is often combined with a small sub-therapeutic amount of atropine to discourage abuse. Clinical indications for motility inhibitors include acute non-specific diarrhoea and chronic diarrhoea associated with irritable bowel syndrome or inflammatory conditions, provided infectious causes have been ruled out. Nursing students must remember that these drugs are strictly contraindicated in infectious diarrhoea caused by invasive organisms such as Shigella, Salmonella, or Clostridium difficile, because slowing motility prevents the clearance of pathogens and toxins, potentially precipitating toxic megacolon. Adverse effects include constipation, abdominal distension, dizziness, and drowsiness. Nurses must monitor bowel sounds, assess for abdominal distension, and educate patients never to exceed the recommended dose.

headings.title: Absorbents and Adsorbents in Diarrhoea Treatment
headings.content: Absorbents and adsorbents act within the gastrointestinal lumen by physically binding to substances such as bacterial toxins, digestive enzymes, and excess fluids, rendering them inactive or facilitating their excretion through faeces. Traditional agents in this group include kaolin, pectin, attapulgite, and activated charcoal. While they have historically been popular in home remedies and over-the-counter formulations across Nigeria, contemporary clinical guidelines suggest they play a minor role compared to rehydration and targeted antimicrobial therapy. One major pharmacokinetic drawback of absorbents and adsorbents is their lack of specificity; they can bind concomitantly administered oral medications, vitamins, and essential nutrients, significantly reducing their systemic absorption and therapeutic efficacy. Therefore, nurses must advise patients to separate the administration of absorbents from other oral drugs by at least two hours. Side effects are generally mild but can include constipation and abdominal discomfort. Nurses play a crucial role in evaluating whether a patient's reliance on over-the-counter adsorbents is masking a more serious underlying condition that requires professional medical diagnosis and intervention.

headings.title: Antisecretory Agents and Antimicrobial Therapy
headings.content: Antisecretory agents and antimicrobial therapies target specific pathological pathways responsible for fluid loss and infection in acute diarrhoeal disease. Racecadotril is a prominent antisecretory drug that acts as a pro-drug, being rapidly converted to thiorphan, an enkephalinase inhibitor. By inhibiting enkephalinase, it prolongs the physiological antisecretory action of endogenous enkephalins in the intestine, effectively reducing the hypersecretion of water and electrolytes into the gut lumen without affecting intestinal motility or transit time. This unique profile makes racecadotril safe for acute watery diarrhoea in both children and adults. In contrast, antimicrobial therapy is reserved for cases where specific bacterial, protozoal, or parasitic agents are identified or strongly suspected based on clinical presentation, such as severe bloody diarrhoea, high fever, or systemic compromise. Common antimicrobials include oral ciprofloxacin or azithromycin for bacterial enteritis, and metronidazole for protozoal infections like giardiasis or amoebiasis. Nursing responsibilities include administering antibiotics strictly around the clock, monitoring for adverse reactions such as superinfections or antibiotic-associated diarrhoea, and educating patients on completing the full prescribed course of treatment to prevent antimicrobial resistance.

headings.title: Oral Rehydration Therapy and Electrolyte Replacement
headings.content: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) is recognized globally by health organizations as the single most important intervention for managing dehydration resulting from acute diarrhoea. ORT utilizes a precisely formulated solution of glucose and electrolytes based on the sodium-glucose cotransport mechanism in the small intestine, where the active transport of glucose drives the simultaneous absorption of sodium and water, even during secretory diarrhoeal states. World Health Organization (WHO) low-osmolarity oral rehydration salts (ORS) have significantly reduced mortality rates, particularly among young children suffering from dehydrating gastroenteritis in resource-limited settings. In cases of severe dehydration, shock, or intractable vomiting where oral intake is impossible, intravenous (IV) fluid resuscitation using isotonic crystalloids such as Normal Saline or Ringer's Lactate is immediately initiated. Nurses must calculate fluid deficit replacement, maintenance requirements, and ongoing losses accurately. Electrolyte monitoring is vital to detect and correct complications such as hyponatremia, hypernatremia, hypokalemia, and metabolic acidosis. Nursing documentation must reflect precise fluid intake and output charts, weights, and clinical signs of hydration status.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Patient Monitoring
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing assessment and rigorous patient monitoring are essential for detecting early signs of clinical deterioration in patients with diarrhoea. The nursing assessment must include a detailed history covering the onset, frequency, consistency, and color of stools, presence of blood or mucus, associated symptoms like fever, nausea, and abdominal cramping, and recent travel or dietary history. Physical assessment focuses heavily on evaluating hydration status, which includes checking skin turgor, mucous membrane moisture, sunken eyes, capillary refill time, level of consciousness, and urine output. Daily weights serve as an objective parameter for monitoring fluid balance fluctuations. Vital signs must be monitored frequently to identify tachycardia, hypotension, or tachypnea, which are hallmark indicators of hypovolemic shock. Nurses must also assess the abdomen for tenderness, distension, and bowel sounds. Any abnormal laboratory findings, such as electrolyte imbalances (particularly potassium and sodium) or elevated serum creatinine pointing to acute kidney injury, must be reported immediately to the attending physician. Systematic documentation ensures continuity of care across shifts and validates the effectiveness of the implemented nursing care plan.

headings.title: Patient Education and Prevention Strategies
headings.content: Patient education and community prevention strategies form the final, crucial line of defense against the burden of diarrhoeal diseases, especially in Nigeria and similar settings where waterborne pathogens are prevalent. Nurses must empower patients and their caregivers with clear instructions on preparing safe oral rehydration solutions at home, recognizing red-flag symptoms (such as blood in the stool, persistent vomiting, high fever, or lethargy), and administering prescribed medications safely. Preventative education should emphasize proper hand hygiene using soap and clean water before eating and after handling waste, safe food handling practices, proper disposal of human waste, and drinking only treated or boiled water. In pediatric populations, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months and the timely introduction of safe complementary foods, alongside zinc supplementation and rotavirus vaccination, have proven highly effective in reducing the incidence and severity of diarrhoeal illness. By actively engaging in health promotion and community outreach, nursing professionals contribute significantly to lowering morbidity and mortality rates associated with gastrointestinal infections.
